pages.title: Proofreading
pages.visualNotes:
DNA polymerase I has separately labeled polymerase and 3' -> 5' proofreading exonuclease active sites. The full figure sequence:

1. A rare tautomeric form of cytosine (**C***), which pairs with A, is incorporated into the growing strand.
2. Before the polymerase moves on, C* shifts back to C; the new nucleotide is now mispaired.
3. The mispaired 3'-OH blocks elongation; polymerase slides back to position the mismatch in the exonuclease active site.
4. The mispaired nucleotide is removed.
5. Polymerase slides forward and resumes polymerization.

pages.title: Mutation: base changes and product effects
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
A mutation is a **permanent change in the nucleotide sequence**. The slide classifies mutations by two aspects:

1. **Nature of the base change:**
   - Substitution: replacement of one or more base pairs with another.
   - Insertion/deletion: addition/deletion of one or more base pairs.
2. **Effect on coding sequence and product:**
   - Silent: affects nonessential DNA or has negligible effect, as worded in the source.
   - Nonsense: premature stop codon.
   - Missense: change in the amino acid encoded.

pages.visualNotes: All four colony photographs reviewed; no invented conditions/counts.
pages.contentMarkdown:
The slide calls the test a rapid, inexpensive screen important in industry.

The slide calls repair energetically inefficient compared with metabolism, where ATP is accounted for and used optimally, emphasizing genetic integrity. pages.title: Mismatch repair and methylation timing
pages.visualNotes: Complete GATC methylation diagram reviewed.
pages.contentMarkdown:
- Mismatch repair improves fidelity by **10^2-10^3**.
- Template methyl groups distinguish template from newly synthesized DNA.
- Repair occurs in the **hemimethylated** interval after replication: template methylated, new strand not methylated.
- The stated lag period is **10 min**.
- **Dam methylase** methylates new-strand **5'-GATC-3'**; both strands then become indistinguishable by this mark.

The diagram follows fully methylated GATC/CTAG through replication, hemimethylation, and Dam action. Its caption says new-strand methylation follows after a few minutes; this qualitative wording and the explicit 10-min annotation are both preserved.

- **MutH binds MutL**; its site-specific endonuclease remains inactive until it encounters unmethylated **5'-GATC-3'**, marking the repair strand.
- Diagram: ATP to ADP + Pi accompanies complex assembly; DNA threads through the complex in both directions until MutH meets unmethylated GATC and cleaves the unmodified strand.

pages.title: Base-excision repair (BER)
pages.visualNotes: Four-panel BER figure reviewed.

uncertainties.description: The diagram labels substrate NTPs while depicting dNMP products. Do not score substrate identity from this ambiguous label.

pages.contentMarkdown:
- **DNA glycosylases** recognize lesions, including A/C-deamination products and lesions caused by environmental agents.
- Removal of a base cleaves the **N-glycosyl bond between base and deoxyribose**, leaving an **apurinic/apyrimidinic (abasic, AP) site**.
- Once an AP site forms it must be repaired.
- **AP endonuclease** cuts the DNA strand containing the AP site.
- The AP-containing segment is removed; **DNA polymerase I** replaces DNA and **ligase** seals the nick.

The four-part diagram shows (a) damaged-base release by glycosylase, (b) AP-endonuclease incision, (c) DNA pol I with NTPs as printed, release of deoxyribose phosphate plus dNMPs, new DNA and a nick, and (d) ligase sealing.

pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
- **UNG** removes U formed by C deamination.
- It distinguishes T from U and acts **only on DNA, not RNA**.
- Bacteria have one type and humans four, as stated.

pages.visualNotes: UV/thymine-dimer figure reviewed.
pages.contentMarkdown:
- Described as critical for all organisms' survival.
- Recognizes **bulky lesions and pyrimidine dimers** causing large DNA-helical distortion.
- A **multisubunit enzyme** hydrolyzes **two phosphodiester bonds**, one on either side of the distortion.
- **Excinuclease** catalyzes two specific endonucleolytic cleavages, distinguished from a standard endonuclease.

The before/after figure shows an incoming **UV photon**, formation of a **thymine dimer**, and distorted DNA.

- One entire protein is consumed per damaged base, emphasizing DNA-integrity priority.
- Diagram: O6-methylguanine nucleotide becomes guanine nucleotide; methyl transfers to the protein's own **Cys-SH**, producing **Cys-S-CH3** and changing protein **active -> inactive**.

pages.visualNotes: DNA pol V and fidelity emphasis reviewed.

uncertainties.description: TLS is placed under Recombinational DNA repair without clarifying the relationship. Do not assess TLS as synonymous with homologous recombination.

Headings combine **Recombinational DNA repair** and **Error-prone translesion DNA synthesis (TLS)**.

- Error-prone means mutations often occur; this is part of the **SOS response**.
- **DNA polymerase V** replicates past/across lesions that normally block replication.
- Proper base pairing is nearly impossible, giving inaccurate repair and high mutation rate.
- Lack of proofreading exonuclease activity reduces fidelity.

pages.title: Three types of DNA recombination
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
DNA recombination: movement of a DNA segment from one DNA molecule to another.

1. **Homologous/general recombination/DNA crossover:** between two homologous molecules.
2. **Site-specific recombination:** at a particular sequence in both nonhomologous molecules.
3. **Transpositional recombination:** a mobile element/short segment inserts into target DNA.

pages.title: Significance of recombination
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:

- Genetic diversity.

The diagram follows **paternal** and **maternal chromosomes** through **DNA replication**, then **crossing over**. A **Meiosis I** bracket covers the following division. Both depicted resulting cells contain duplicated chromosomes with exchanged colored parental segments.

pages.visualNotes: All three chromosome panels reviewed.

Panels (a)-(c) label **homologous pair**, **sister chromatids**, **centromere**, and **chiasma**; exchanged terminal segments use different colors.

Crossing over exchanges genetic material.

pages.title: Double-strand break repair system
pages.visualNotes: Full diagram prose and both alternative products read.
pages.contentMarkdown:
Most damage is described as BER/NER-repaired, but replication forks encounter breaks. Two homologous chromosomes participate:

1. A double-strand break becomes a gap through exonuclease action. More removal at **5' ends** leaves **3' single-stranded extensions**; the diagram says strands with 3' ends degrade less than strands with 5' ends.
2. An exposed 3' end invades and pairs with its complement in an intact homolog, displacing the other duplex strand.
3. DNA polymerase extends the invading 3' end; **branch migration** yields two crossovers/**Holliday intermediates**.
4. Further replication replaces DNA missing from the original break.
5. Specialized nucleases cleave the intermediates, producing **either of two joining products**.

The diagram labels **Gene A/Gene B**, strand ends, and **product set 1/product set 2**. In product set 2, DNA on either side of the repaired region is recombined. These are alternative outcomes, not one uniquely required product.

pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:

- Both cleavage products occur in vivo in eukaryotes and prokaryotes, contributing to genomic diversity.
- Homologous chromosomes are not identical; alleles may differ.
- Example: **hemoglobin A** versus **hemoglobin S (sickle cell anemia)**. The source states **A to T = glutamate to valine** and emphasizes a one-base-pair difference among millions.

- A fork moving origin to terminus can encounter double-strand breaks/lesions despite BER/NER repair of most damage.
- **DNA polymerase III cannot continue**, leading to recombinational repair.
- **Origin-independent restart** is described using a **complex of 7 proteins**, listed **(priA, C, DnaB, C, G, T)**, followed by **DNA polymerase II**.
- Summary: **replication -> recombinational repair -> replication** for a stalled/blocked fork.

pages.visualNotes: All four reaction panels and chemical labels reviewed.
pages.contentMarkdown:
- **Recombinase/integrase** acts at a **20-200 bp** recombination site.
- The site-specific enzyme is a **tetramer of identical units**.
- The source says one recombinase recognizes/binds each of two sites through phosphotyrosine.
- A transient protein-DNA covalent linkage preserves the phosphodiester linkage through **phosphoserine/phosphotyrosine**, as worded.
- Recombinase = **site-specific endonuclease + ligase**.

Numbered reaction panels (1)-(4) show **tyrosine OH** as nucleophile in strand cleavage, Tyr-phosphate intermediates, free OH, joining to new partners to form a **Holliday intermediate**, then remaining-strand cleavage/rejoining. Strands retain 5'/3' labels and mixed recombinant colors.

pages.title: Transpositional recombination and element classes
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
Transpositional recombination inserts a **mobile element** into target DNA.

- **Simple transposons:** contain only sequence required for transposition, including transposase genes.
- **Complex transposons:** contain one or more additional genes; **antibiotic resistance** is the example.

pages.visualNotes: Both transposition routes reviewed.

| **Class II: transposons** | A special enzyme cuts donor transposon, then it inserts in target DNA; **transposase** has nuclease and ligase activities |

Paired figure:

- Transposon: **donor DNA -> cut by transposase -> DNA intermediate -> recombination -> target DNA**.
- Retrotransposon: **donor DNA -> transcription -> RNA -> reverse transcription -> DNA intermediate -> recombination -> target DNA**.

pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.

Three RNA classes have different, complementary roles in protein synthesis (translation):

| RNA | Role stated |

| tRNA | Transmits code and delivers the specified amino acid |
| rRNA | Associates with proteins to form **ribosomes**, protein-synthesizing machines |

pages.title: Transcription versus replication
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
The source comparison lists:

1. Similar chemical reaction/mechanism: **PPi hydrolysis** drives synthesis forward.
2. Stages: initiation, elongation, termination.
3. Template needed.
4. Synthesis polarity **5' to 3'**.
5. Transcription requires **no primer**.
6. Transcription covers a **limited DNA segment**.
7. Transcription has **no 3' to 5' proofreading activity** and cannot excise mismatched nucleotides, as stated.

pages.title: Transcription requirements
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
1. **RNA polymerase**.
2. **DNA template**, the 3' to 5' strand.
3. **No primer required**.
4. Nucleoside triphosphates **ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP**.
5. Synthesis **5' to 3'**.
6. **Mg2+ and Zn2+**.

pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.

**(NMP)n + NTP -> (NMP)n+1 + PPi**

The initial polymer is labeled **RNA**, the product **lengthened RNA**.

pages.title: DNA-dependent synthesis of RNA
pages.visualNotes: All bubble/strand labels and 3-prime-OH annotation reviewed.
pages.contentMarkdown:
RNA polymerase adds ribonucleotide units to the **3'-hydroxyl end**, building RNA **5' to 3'**.

- Nucleotides are selected by Watson-Crick pairing; base-pair geometry contributes to selection.
- The 3' OH at the active site acts as nucleophile attacking the phosphate of incoming **rNTP**.
- Figure labels: **transcription bubble**, **nontemplate strand**, **template strand**, **RNA polymerase**, **active site**, **RNA-DNA hybrid, 8 bp**, emerging RNA 5' end.
- In the depicted left-to-right transcription direction, DNA **unwinds ahead** at right and **rewinds behind** at left.

pages.title: Stages of transcription
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
- **Initiation:** starts at a promoter; RNA polymerase binds specific DNA sequences.
- **Elongation:** growing RNA temporarily pairs with the template as a short **8 bp RNA-DNA hybrid**; hybrid peels off and the DNA duplex reforms. Rate: **50-90 nucleotides/s**.
- **Termination:** named as the third stage; mechanisms follow on later pages.

pages.title: Transcription and DNA supercoiling
pages.visualNotes: Supercoil signs and spatial relationships checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
Because DNA is helical, transcription-bubble movement requires strand rotation, causing supercoiling in vitro and in vivo; **topoisomerase** relieves it.

The left-to-right figure depicts **negative supercoils behind** the transcription complex and **positive supercoils ahead**, labels emerging RNA 5' end, and annotates **17 bp unwound, 8 bp DNA-RNA hybrid**.

2. **Initiation:** transcription begins; complex moves away from promoter (**promoter clearance**).
3. **Elongation:** **sigma dissociates** and polymerase leaves the promoter.

- Bacteria have two principal mechanisms involving RNA polymerase; one additionally requires **Rho**.
- Eukaryotic termination mechanisms differ among the **three RNA polymerases**.

- It proceeds along mRNA and probably outraces/catches up to RNA polymerase, as worded.
- Its **ATP-dependent helicase activity** disrupts the RNA-DNA hybrid.
- Termination completes with release of Rho and RNA polymerase from nucleic acids.

pages.title: Post-transcriptional processing in eukaryotes
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
- Genes are transcribed in the **nucleus** to RNA.
- In the nucleus, mRNA is **spliced**, **5'-capped**, and **3'-polyadenylated**.
- mRNA is transported to the **cytoplasm for translation**.

pages.title: Three eukaryotic mRNA modifications
pages.visualNotes: Text visually checked.
pages.contentMarkdown:
1. **Capping:** modified **5' cap** residue is added at the 5' end before transcription ends.
2. **Splicing:** introns are removed and exons joined. **Alternative splicing** allows some transcripts to be spliced in more than one way and has regulatory significance.
3. **Polyadenylation:** the 3' end is cleaved and **80-250 A residues** are added as a **poly(A) tail**.

The source states these modifications work together with **phosphorylated CTD and RNA polymerase II**. The list enumerates modification types and does not establish a unique chronological order for all three processes.

pages.title: Primary transcript to mature mRNA diagram
pages.visualNotes: Image-only teaching page fully reviewed, including all labels and dashed exon guides.
pages.contentMarkdown:
The diagram explicitly connects these stages:

1. **Transcription and 5' capping:** RNA polymerase moves along DNA, leaving emerging RNA labeled **5' cap**, **exon** and **intron**.
2. **Completion of primary transcript:** a **primary transcript** contains the cap, alternating exon/intron segments, and a **noncoding end sequence** toward the **3'** end.
3. **Cleavage, polyadenylation, and splicing:** introns loop out and are removed; dashed guides show retained exon segments joining, while end cleavage and poly(A) addition are grouped with splicing.
4. **Mature mRNA:** joined exon segments retain the **5' cap**, noncoding end segment and **AAA(A)n** at the **3'** end.

These grouped operations do not justify requiring an arbitrary unique order among cleavage, polyadenylation and individual splicing events.
